evals.prompt: I organize DevRhein Conf, a volunteer-run developer conference in Cologne that happens every year. Our video volunteer published all 24 talks on YouTube last week, so the masters are done. The team is completely wiped and basically dissolves after next week - I personally have maybe one free afternoon a week at best, and nobody else has committed to anything past the event. I read everywhere that dripping content keeps engagement alive, so my plan is to release one clip per week for the next 24 weeks. One wrinkle: our headline sponsor's report is due in six weeks and it needs to show post-event content actually went out. Can you draft the release plan for me?
evals.expected_output: A release plan that rejects the 24-week drip, recommends a batched release (or dated dump) pinned to the six-week sponsor deadline, with the write-up first, a date and named owner on every line, and no view targets.
expectations: Rejects the proposed one-clip-per-week drip over 24 weeks
States that a drip requires both a recurring edition and a named owner with a standing slot through a stated end date, and identifies that the owner half is missing here
Does not treat the annual recurrence alone as sufficient to justify the drip
Recommends a batched release (or an all-at-once dump) as the latency choice for this team
Evaluates latency options on whether planned artifacts actually ship (completion), not on reach or sustained presence alone
Names the specific failure that the later half of a drip is what an exhausted post-event team drops
Refuses any 'we will publish when we get to it' arrangement as an option, rather than presenting it as the cheapest choice
States that an all-at-once dump with a date is the acceptable floor, not a failure
Places the written write-up in the first wave, before any clips
Every line of the plan carries the artifact, a date, and a named person
Uses the six-week sponsor-report deadline to pin the release dates
Treats evergreen re-surfacing only as opportunistic re-posting of already-existing artifacts with no schedule, or excludes it because nobody will keep the watch
Presents the plan (sessions, formats, dates) for validation before any editing starts

evals.prompt: MeshLayer Summit was a one-time conference our company ran - leadership already decided there won't be a second edition. All 28 talks are live on the event's channel. My repurposing plan: (1) fully corrected transcripts of all 28 talks as web pages, (2) launch a podcast feed from the talk audio - we don't have a podcast today but the audio is basically free since it's already separated, (3) clips of every talk in programme order starting with the opening keynote. Our feedback forms show three sessions people would not stop asking about: the Rust rewrite talk, the incident-review talk, and the accessibility talk. I have one half-time marketing person for one month. What order do we do this in?
evals.expected_output: A derivative mix led by a written write-up plus clips of the three most-asked-about sessions, rejecting the podcast (no standing property) and the 28 transcript pages (one-off edition), with the consent record checked before formats are committed.
expectations: Leads the derivative mix with a written write-up
Restricts clips to the three sessions people asked about rather than clipping all 28 in programme order
Rejects or defers the audio-cut/podcast plan because no standing audio property with its own subscribers exists
States the audio cut has nowhere to land on its own, or that the write-up is strictly better on both value and effort
Notes that building a standing podcast or channel is a separate undertaking beyond a single edition's repurposing, not part of this plan
Rejects transcript pages for all 28 talks because the edition does not recur (and search-driven discovery is unestablished), so the per-talk correction pass does not pay back
Identifies the transcript correction pass as a standing job across a programme, not a quick automated export
Warns against publishing an uncorrected machine transcript as if it were a finished document
Directs the write-up to cover what the sessions actually said, not to restate the schedule or programme
Has the write-up link to the published masters rather than re-hosting the videos
Checks the consent record and marks sessions before committing to any format
Does not set a view, download, or engagement target for any derivative

evals.prompt: OpsWharf Days wrapped two weeks ago and the 12 talks are on the event's YouTube channel, which only has about 900 subscribers. My plan: besides cutting a few highlight clips, re-upload all 12 full talks to our main company brand channel and as LinkedIn native video, with new thumbnails and our company intro bumper, since that's where the audience actually is. Can you also write the captions and pick hashtags for each clip? And once everything's produced I'll just drop the Google Drive folder link in the #marketing Slack channel so the team planning next year's push can dig through it all.
evals.expected_output: Refusal of the full-talk re-upload as repurposing, real derivatives kept instead, captions/hashtags handed to the channel owner with a structured per-piece handover, and a curated inventory list replacing the shared folder.
expectations: Refuses to treat re-uploading the full talks to the brand channel and LinkedIn as repurposing, stating a full-session re-upload is the master again, not a derivative
Names the risk that a second copy published under different terms stops matching the consent record, or splits the archive
States that the master file and its publication belong to the production pipeline, not to this repurposing work
Keeps actual derivatives (clips, a write-up) as the deliverable instead of the re-upload
Declines to write the captions, pick the hashtags, or choose platforms, handing those to whoever runs the event's channels
Hands each scheduled piece over with the artifact and where its file is
The handover carries the publish date for each piece
The handover carries the licence line that must appear with each piece
The handover carries any rights restriction per piece (a speaker not to tag, a photo not to use, frames already cut)
Replaces the shared drive-folder link with a curated inventory list for the next edition's campaign
The inventory marks which artifacts are evergreen versus dated, and which carry an open licence and which do not
The inventory names what is missing and will not exist, so the next campaign is not built on a hoped-for piece

evals.prompt: StackHarbor Conf's speaker release says talks 'may be recorded and published on the conference's channels' - all 30 speakers signed it except our two workshop hosts, who never returned the form. One speaker signed but only on the condition that slide 14, which shows customer data, stays out of anything public. The full recordings are up. We now want 60-second vertical cuts of the best moments plus Portuguese subtitle tracks for the whole programme. Consent is already sorted since everyone knew about the cameras and chose to speak, so this should be quick - can you plan the cuts?
evals.expected_output: A per-session usable/restricted/off-limits list: publication-only sessions restricted (link, don't cut), the two unsigned sessions off-limits, the slide-14 condition carried, and the release-form gap routed upstream for next edition.
expectations: States that a grant of recording and publication does not license re-cuts or derivative works
Treats both the vertical cuts and the translated subtitle tracks as derivative works that exceed the publication grant
Marks the sessions covered by the publication-only release as restricted rather than usable
For restricted sessions, links to the published master instead of cutting from it
Marks the two workshop sessions with no returned form as off-limits, stating that silence is not permission
Rejects the 'everyone knew about the cameras' argument - a camera in the room is not agreement
Carries the slide-14 condition as a named restriction on that speaker's session
Produces a written three-state list (usable / restricted / off-limits) before any format is chosen
Routes the release-form gap to whoever owns consent collection, as wording added to the next edition's release
Does not itself re-contact speakers to collect new consent or build a parallel consent flow
Runs this check before production and editing, not at publication time
States that a derivative of an uncovered recording is as unpublishable as the recording itself
Notes that some events' releases do extend explicitly to editing and derivative works, so the fix is a release-form change rather than an impossibility

evals.prompt: Three clip candidates from ForgeData Summit, all already cut - our editor spent a full day on them. Clip A: a live demo where Spotify is audibly playing a licensed track for 40 seconds right through the best moment. Clip B: a talk where a competitor's dashboard is on screen for most of the demo. Clip C: a slide with a chart lifted from an analyst firm's paid report. The editor says short excerpts from a nonprofit conference are fair use, and worst case YouTube just mutes the audio. Green light to publish all three?
evals.expected_output: No green light: each finding gets one of clear/cut/drop, the music clip is dropped unless cleared (no partial version), the gate is moved before cutting for future clips, and the fair-use hand-wave is rejected.
expectations: Refuses to publish and see what happens (muting, complaints, takedown) as a strategy
Rejects the blanket fair-use justification as a substitute for clearance
Offers exactly three actions per finding: clear it with the rights holder, cut those frames, or drop the clip
For the clip where the licensed track runs through the key moment: drop the clip unless the music is cleared, with no partial version
Treats the competitor's on-screen interface as third-party material requiring review, not as automatically safe
Treats the chart from the analyst report as third-party published work requiring review
Points out the rights gate should have run before cutting, and that the editor's day of work is the cost of checking at upload time
Applies the third-party checklist per planned clip before production going forward
States that third-party clearance for slide material has no owner, and that the checklist is deliberately minimal rather than clearance advice
Notes a third-party finding is reversible (the piece can be re-cut without those frames), unlike publishing an identifiable attendee
Keeps the source files and a record of what was cut and why
Does not treat the speaker's own consent as covering the third-party material in their slides or demo

evals.prompt: KernelBloom Fest used red-dot stickers on badges for people who didn't want to be photographed. Our photographer delivered about 900 photos, but the stickers aren't legible in most shots and there's no per-photo log of who opted out. Marketing wants an Instagram carousel of the best close-ups - people laughing at the workshop tables, hallway conversations, that kind of energy. Nobody complained during or after the event, and our code of conduct already covers photography, so legally I think we're covered. Which photos do we pick?
evals.expected_output: Close crops ruled out: with the opt-out unretrievable per photo the set is restricted to wide shots where nobody is identifiable (or unused), the no-complaints and code-of-conduct arguments are rejected, and no substitute consent mechanism is invented.
expectations: Rules out the close-up carousel: with the opt-out not retrievable per photo, the whole set is restricted for identifiable close crops
Allows at most wide shots where nobody is identifiable, or recommends not using the set at all
Rejects 'nobody complained' as permission - silence at publishing time is not consent
States the opt-out signal was given in a moment that has passed and cannot be re-collected, so re-asking the room is not available
States that a published face cannot be recalled from copies already made
Treats identifiable-attendee material as the heaviest rights category, above third-party material in slides
Rejects the code-of-conduct argument: its text prohibits harassing photography and carries no photo-consent mechanism
Does not attribute a photo-consent policy to the code of conduct that the event never adopted
Does not invent a substitute consent mechanism (such as emailing attendees for retroactive approval) parallel to the badge signal
Treats the badge-sticker scheme as the only attendee-photo signal, owned by the accessibility/inclusion side of the event rather than by this workstream
Runs the photo check before production and selection, not just before publication
Recommends deciding the photo-set policy at planning time rather than after pieces are edited

evals.prompt: For LensStack Conf we want to open-license everything - TED puts Creative Commons on all their talks, so it seems like the standard conferences follow. Plan: CC BY 4.0 across the board - the talk recordings, the transcript pages, and the photo set. One complication: about a third of the speakers are still on last year's release, which only covers publication, and several talks have vendor product screenshots in the demos. To keep the artifacts clean we'd note the licence in our internal spreadsheet and the press kit rather than stamping it on each file. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: A licence decision that treats TED as one event's own choice not a standard, refuses CC over publication-only sessions and screenshot-carrying derivatives, splits terms per artifact and per session, puts the licence line on each artifact, and records who decided.
expectations: States that conferences follow no shared licence convention and treats TED's choice as one event's own, not a standard to match
If TED's licence is characterized, gets it right as CC BY-NC-ND (no commercial use, no derivative works) rather than a permissive licence like CC BY
Refuses CC BY over the talks whose release covers publication only, on the ground that you cannot grant more than the consent record gave
Flags that an open licence on a derivative containing vendor screenshots licenses somebody else's work along with the event's
Where either constraint bites, publishes without an open licence and states that explicitly rather than leaving terms unstated
Notes that an artifact with no licence line and no statement gets resolved in the re-user's favour
Considers different terms per artifact type - recording, transcript, and photo have different rights-holders behind them
Advises that the sessions under the derivative-covering release may carry the open licence while the publication-only third does not, rather than an all-or-nothing call
Puts the licence line on each artifact where a re-user will actually see it, not only in a spreadsheet or press kit
Records who made the licence decision
Makes the licence call explicitly as this workstream's own decision rather than deferring it or letting it drift
Rejects deciding the licence per artifact at upload time by whoever uploads, which produces an archive with mixed unrecorded terms

evals.prompt: Six clips from PortAndAdapter Conf are live. This week I want to: (1) email all 30 speakers their full-talk video link plus their clip and ask everyone to share; (2) for our keynote speaker, who has 120k followers, just tag her on the event's post - she'll see it; (3) put targets in the sponsor report: 10,000 views per clip and 50% of speakers sharing. Two of the six clips haven't been reviewed by anyone yet, including the speakers, but send those asks anyway - they'll love seeing themselves. Oh, and one of the clips is a teaser from a workshop whose host never signed the release, but it's only 20 seconds. Draft the outreach?
evals.expected_output: A scoped speaker ask: no video-link mass email, a one-line ask on the existing follow-up as default with ready-made assets for the most-asked sessions, a conditional dated joint push for the keynote, no ask on unseen cuts, the unsigned teaser pulled, and view targets refused in favour of self-set measures.
expectations: Drops sending speakers their own full-talk video links - that message belongs to the post-event follow-up someone else already owns
Scopes the outreach to the derivative made from each speaker's own talk, and nothing else
Defaults to a one-line ask riding the follow-up message already being sent, coordinating the wording rather than sending a separate message to all 30
Upgrades to a ready-made asset (clip plus drafted caption and link) only for the speakers of the most-asked-about sessions, not for everyone
Grounds the ready-made asset in the reasoning that the speaker's own effort, not their willingness, decides whether they post
For the 120k-follower keynote speaker, proposes a dated joint push (same-day, cross-tagged) conditional on her agreeing to a date, instead of just tagging her
Refuses to ask any speaker to amplify a clip they have not seen - the two unreviewed clips get no ask until the speaker has seen the cut
Reuses the event's existing shareable kit rather than building a second one
Refuses the 10,000-views-per-clip target and does not invent any numeric view, retention, or engagement threshold
Offers self-set measures instead, such as amplification take-up (speakers who posted over speakers asked)
Reads a low take-up rate as diagnosing the ask (usually a missing attached asset), not the speakers
Cites the checkable completeness gates: every derivative traces to a consent-covered session, and every artifact had a date and an owner before production
Flags the teaser from the unsigned workshop as unpublishable regardless of length, and sends that host no amplification ask
